paragraphs.text: "Grandpa?" Laurie called, knocking on the study door. "It's dinnertime!" She opened the door and found Grandpa bent over his desk, as usual. He was an archaeologist and worked very hard. When he wasn't out traveling and researching, he was home in his study. "What are you doing, Grandpa?"
"I’m tracing an ancient map of Mesopotamia," he said.
"Meso-what?" Laurie peeked over his shoulder and saw a piece of tracing paper covered in wavy lines. Two lines were drawn in blue and made a sort of V. "What are those two squiggly lines?"

"Mesopotamia was the name of a region in the Middle East, where human civilization arose thousands of years ago. These two lines are the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Thanks to them, humans in that area had water for farming, fish to eat, and mud and reeds to build houses. You may have heard of the Sumerians. They were the most powerful people there—in what became known as the cradle of civilization. The Sumerians may have lived in mud houses, but they were very sophisticated and we owe a lot to their inventions. For example, they developed the first writing system!

"They began writing with pictures. So to indicate a star, they would draw a picture of a star. And water would be written by drawing wavy lines, like the waves in the Tigris and Euphrates. Later they developed those pictures into symbols that represented ideas or objects. Eventually they created signs to represent the sounds of their language. Their writing looks choppy because it was pressed into clay tablets using thin tools made from reeds. After that they baked the tablets in the sun.

"In addition to being masters of language, the Sumerians were clever mathematicians who tried to use numbers to organize the world around them. They were especially keen on dividing time. Our calendarㅡwith a 30-day month, 7-day week, 24-hour day, 60-minute hour, and 60-second minuteㅡis based on their math! Can you believe we owe so much to people who lived over five thousand years ago?"
"No, but I can believe Mom will be mad at us if we don't go downstairs and eat dinner," Laurie said.
"Your mother is like the great King Hammurabi of ancient Babylonia, which was an area of Mesopotamia," Grandpa said. "She lays down the laws around here!"
"I've heard of him! Wasn't he the scary king who asked for an 'eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth'?" Laurie shuddered.

"Yes, I guess we might say he sounds scary now. But Hammurabi's laws kept society in order at a time when there was lots of fighting between tribes. I think his laws are interesting because they teach us about what was considered important in ancient Mesopotamia. For example, we know that people were expected to take responsibility for their work and actions. If a house collapsed and killed the people inside, the builder was put to death. But unfortunately, punishment wasn't always as clear-cut as it sounds. You were often able to escape a harsh sentence by paying a large fine. In ancient Babylonia it helped to be wealthy.

"Would you like to see pictures of Babylonia's capital? It was called Babylon and was one of the most impressive cities in Mesopotamia. Those huge structures are called ziggurats. They were built entirely out of mud bricks. They were probably very difficult to build. People took great care in building them, however, because they were made for worshipping gods. The steep sides were stepped and covered with beautiful gardens. At the top was a shrine. The most famous ziggurat is the temple to the god Marduk in the city of Ur. You recall the Tower of Babel from the Bible, don't you? In that story people tried to build a tower that would reach the heavens, but they failed in the end. Some believe the ziggurat in Ur is the basis of the biblical legend.

"The city of Ur, which is in present-day Iraq, is thought to connect to other stories from the Bible as well. It was the home of Abraham, and when archaeologists first discovered the ruins of Ur in the 1800s, they found evidence of a great flood that had likely wiped out most of the city. They believe this may have been the basis of the great flood story in the Bible as well. You know, the one that led to Noah building his ark.

"Wait a minute. I have something to show you from the excavation at Ur. A British archaeologist uncovered some of the grandest treasures of the ancient world when he found the temples and cemetery there in the 1920s and ’30s. The tomb of Lady Puabi, for example, was full of beautiful things. This royal woman was buried with all her riches, and was covered from head to foot in jewels and gold. Lady Puabi's real headdress is in a museum, but I have a replica. A replica is something that's made to look exactly like the real thing. Try this on for size, Lady Laurie."
Grandpa leaned over and placed a delicate headdress decorated with dangling golden leaves, rings, and flowers on Laurie's head.
"Laurie, didn't I send you to call Grandpa for dinner ten minutes ago?" Laurie's mom shouted. "What are you two doing up there? Dinner is getting cold!"
"That's Lady Laurie to you, Mom!" Laurie said. She turned on her heel and strode out the door, her headdress jingling.
Laurie had just come home from school when she heard a light hammering sound coming from Grandpa’s study. Curious, she tapped on the door. "Grandpa? Can I come in?"
"Just a second!" Grandpa answered. Laurie heard lots of shuffling. "Enter!"
Grandpa was sitting empty-handed at his desk, but there were wood shavings everywhere. "Aren’t you supposed to be at school?" he asked.
"It’s over at three. What were you doing in here?" Laurie said suspiciously. She saw something wooden poking out from underneath a book. "Aha!" she cried, pulling the object out. "What’s this?"
"Well, Miss Nosy, that’s your birthday present. But now it won’t be a surprise," Grandpa said.
It was a wooden crocodile with a string attached to the top of its head so the mouth could be opened and shut. Laurie pulled the string and snapped the crocodile’s jaws.

"It’s an ancient Egyptian toy," Grandpa said. "I made this, but if you were a child in ancient Egypt, you might have something similar. Crocodiles were a significant part of Egyptian life because the civilization was built along the Nile River, and many crocodiles lived there. The Egyptian civilization has been called the gift of the Nile, because the Egyptians depended on the river for many things, including irrigation and fertilizer. It flooded every year, supplying much-needed water and nutrients to the surrounding land. This made farming easy for the Egyptians. The soft, wet land also made good mud for building mud-brick houses. And the river unified the people of the area by providing a convenient highway for transportation and communication.

"Ancient Egypt was an agricultural society. Do you know what that means? It means life depended heavily on farming. If you were a little Egyptian girl living about four thousand years ago, your father would probably be a grain farmer. Grains were the most common crop, especially wheat and barley, which were used to make bread and beer—the most typical food and drink.

"Unfortunately children didn’t get to go to school like you do now. You’d probably spend most days helping your parents. During harvest season maybe you would bundle wheat on the farm. Or perhaps you’d be at home, helping to cook or take care of the vegetable garden near your house.
"But Egypt wasn’t all farms. If you were a well-to-do Egyptian family, you might live near a city," Grandpa said, looking around his desk. He handed Laurie a drawing of an ancient Egyptian city.
"What’s this big thing?" Laurie asked, pointing to a large structure rising above palm trees. "And what’s that funny picture of a bird with a beach ball?"

"That’s the temple to the sun god, Ra. He was the most important god, as the Egyptians thought he was responsible for the rising sun, which brought light and nourishment to their land. Many temples were built in worship to him. And that’s not a bird with a beach ball! That’s ‘Ra’ in hieroglyphics, an ancient form of writing. Just as the sun looks different throughout the day, Ra appeared in many different forms. But most often he was shown as a falcon carrying the great, big sun over his head. Every morning he rose from underground and traveled across the sky in a boat. And every evening he went back beneath the ground. He had the most important job of all—creator of the universe.

"The next most important job was that of the pharaoh, the Egyptian king. Pharaohs were considered part god. They were in charge of politics, the military, and the welfare of their citizens. They were also the link between the gods and humans. Without the pharaoh, Egyptians thought, the world would end up in chaos! But the pharaohs lived a life of luxury compared to common farmers.They owned most of the land, lived in huge palaces with many servants, and could get whatever they wanted.

"Both their responsibilities and wealth continued after death too. When a pharaoh died, Egyptians believed he became the king of the dead and buried him in an elaborate tomb. In order for him to be able to perform his duties properly, he had to be buried with everything he would need. This included his body, which was preserved, and his most valuable possessions. Inside the tomb the walls were also covered with paintings of slaves, food, and animals. You’ve seen pictures of the pyramids of Giza, right? Those magnificent structures were tombs for pharaohs!

"The tomb paintings have taught us a lot about the Egyptians. For example, one of their favorite sports was hunting. Egyptians are thought to be the first people to hunt purely for pleasure. The area around the Nile was full of wildlife; they hunted birds, gazelles, lions, and hippopotamuses! Hippo hunts seem to have been particularly popular. Hippos, you know, live mostly in the water. Egyptians hunted them with long spears from boats.
"Hippo ahead!" Grandpa cried, jumping up and pretending to spot something in the distance. "Attack!" he yelled as he hurled an imaginary spear into the air.
"Grandpa, did they hunt crocodiles?" Laurie asked worriedly, holding the toy on her palm.

Grandpa returned from his fantasy hippo hunt and looked at Laurie. "Well, I haven’t seen any pictures of it, but hunting dangerous animals was a way to earn respect. And crocodiles are pretty dangerous. But crocodiles were associated with the water god, whom Egyptians both feared and honored. So perhaps your little crocodile would have been spared." Grandpa smiled and tapped the crocodile on its head. Laurie smiled too.
"Laurie! I’m home!" Mom called from downstairs.
"Hi, Mom! I’ll be right down!" Laurie hollered back. "Thanks, Grandpa. I’ll pretend I never saw this," she said, putting the crocodile back on the desk. "Until next time!"
"Until next time! Bye, Laurie!"

"Grandpa, we're home!" Laurie shouted as she ran up the stairs. She had just come back from the beach with her dad and was carrying a jar full of seashells. "Choose any one you like, but only one," she said, standing at the study door.
"Thank you!" Grandpa said, examining the shells closely. He took a small peach-colored shell from the jar. "I'll add this to my collection."
"You have a shell collection too?" Laurie asked.

"Well, I have just two shells, but they are very special ones from Lebanon!" Grandpa reached high on a shelf and took down a bowl with two spiny seashells in it. "These are sea-snail shells from the Mediterranean coastline. I found them when I visited Lebanon last year to research the ancient Phoenicians. They were seafaring merchants who lived there from around 2000 BC to 500 BC, when they were taken over by the Persian Empire."
"What are seafaring merchants?" said Laurie.

"People who spend a lot of time sailing at sea and make their living by trading things," Grandpa explained. "The coasts of Lebanon are surrounded by high, rugged mountains, which protected Phoenicia, but it also made it difficult to travel by land. So, out of necessity, the Phoenicians became great shipbuilders and seafarers. From their coastal cities, they sailed to other Middle Eastern cities, and to Africa and Europe. There, they traded their goods for things they couldn't find in their homeland. They are considered the first organized traders and merchants of the world.

"Even though we call them Phoenicians and the area they lived in Phoenicia, they weren't really united into a country or empire. Phoenicia was more like individual cities that developed close to one another. But when the Phoenicians traveled around selling their goods, they became known as one people, the Phoenicians."
"Did they simply sell these seashells by the seashore?" Laurie asked, giggling.

"No, silly, but the sea snails that came from these seashells—whew!—were the source of the Phoenicians' most valuable item: purple dye. Purple dye hadn't yet been discovered anywhere else, and when the Phoenicians began to make cloth dyed this wonderful purple, people loved it. But hundreds of snails were needed to dye even a small piece of fabric. So the dye-making process was very time-consuming, and therefore, the dye was worth a lot of money. It was so expensive that only royalty or the very wealthy could afford anything purple. That's how purple became known as the 'royal' color.

"Glass and cedarwood were also popular Phoenician items. Cedar, which grew in the mountains of Lebanon, was rare in neighboring lands; that made it highly desirable. It was also perfect for building and produced great-smelling oils. The Egyptians in particular bought lots of cedar, which they used to build temples, palaces, and coffins. The Phoenicians' seaside location helped them with something else—glassmaking, because glass is made with sand. People think Egyptians had been making glass for a while, but the Phoenicians developed it into an art. They made colored beads, clear vases, and other beautiful glasswork.

"We owe a lot to the Phoenicians for their creations. But they are most famous for one thing. You know, as merchants, it was important for them to keep records of all their sales. What do you think they invented to help them do this?" Grandpa paused.
"Hmm . . . receipts?" Laurie guessed.

"Well, yes, but how would they write receipts if they didn't have an alphabet? The Phoenicians invented the first 22-letter alphabet! Of course, written language had gradually been developing since the time of picture symbols, like hieroglyphics, but the Phoenicians created the first letters representing sound alone. We can even trace our alphabet back to theirs! Here, what do you think this says?" Grandpa wrote three Phoenician letters on a piece of paper.
"Um, triangle, circle, cross . . . D-O-T! Dot!" Laurie cried excitedly.
"Amazing! You can read Phoenician!" Grandpa laughed. He handed her an open book from his desk. The page showed a chart of the Phoenician alphabet.

"Wow. Letters have come a long way in three thousand years. I wonder what they'll look like three thousand years from now!" Laurie said. She flipped to another page in the book. "Ooh, who is this? She's beautiful!" she whispered.

"That's Jezebel, princess of Tyre. Tyre was a city on Phoenicia's coast. It was one of the richest, most powerful Phoenician cities. The king of Tyre married his beautiful daughter to the king of Israel's son, Ahab. He thought this would keep good relations between the two neighboring peoples, but he was wrong. In Israel, the Jewish people worshipped one god, while Phoenicians worshipped a number of gods and goddesses, who they believed controlled weather, harvests, the sea, the moon, and so on—in other words, the natural world.

"Now, Jezebel was a passionate woman who loved her husband but loved her native religion more. She asked Ahab to build temples to her gods and goddesses in his land, and she encouraged the people of Israel to join her in worship. The Jewish leaders got upset. They destroyed the Phoenician temples and killed the Phoenician priests. In all the political turmoil, Ahab and Jezebel were also killed." Grandpa sighed. "Wow! What a story for a beautiful Saturday afternoon!"
"Oh! Why do strong women in history always die tragically?" Laurie cried.
"One day soon, I'll have a story for you about a strong woman who lives to see a happy end," said Grandpa.

"Well, I'm going to put this stuff in my room now. But I'll always think of crushed sea snails when I wear my purple tank top and of that ancient, funny-looking alphabet when I'm writing! And you can have another seashell. Catch!" Laurie said. She tossed another shell from her jar to Grandpa and walked out the door.

Laurie was in Grandpa’s study, looking for a book she needed for her history report. "Aha!" she said, grabbing a book called Alexander the Great . Just then a leather-bound journal caught her eye. When she pulled it from the shelf, a photograph fluttered to the floor. It was a photo of Grandpa standing among mysterious stone doorways. Grandpa looked very young.
The title page of the journal read: Persepolis, 1979 . It was written in Grandpa’s handwriting. Laurie turned the page and started reading.
"'Jim and I just arrived in Iran this morning. The drive from the airport was uneventful but hot. I spent the whole bus ride wondering what the scenery might have looked like back in 500 BC—’"
"Laurie?" Grandpa suddenly appeared in the doorway.
"You scared me!" Laurie cried, slamming the journal shut.

"What are you reading?" he asked. "Ah, my journal from Iran! Your great-uncle Jim and I went to Persepolis the year it was declared a UNESCO World Heritage site. We had a terrific time exploring the ruins there."
"What is Persepolis?" asked Laurie.

"It was the capital of the Persian Empire, which was the largest empire in the world from 559 BC to 330 BC. It covered most of the Middle East, from Egypt to India, and was made up of many different provinces. Although Persian rulers tried to do something impossible—unite the known world under one power—they were nearly successful because they allowed the conquered people to keep their freedoms. In fact, some call the Cyrus Cylinder—an ancient Persian document written on a clay cylinder—the first declaration of human rights. It describes how Cyrus let the people in his empire have freedom of culture and religion.

"The ruler who founded the empire and conquered much of its territory was Cyrus the Great. Many say he began the age of world-empire building, which would continue with the Greeks and Romans. He had some good ideas about how to create and control an empire. For example, he knew it was important to make sure the people you conquered were happy so they would not rise up against you. So when Cyrus marched his troops into Babylon in 539 BC, he did not burn buildings, steal from people’s homes, or run around killing people. He became known as a peaceful and generous ruler. He also freed the Jews who were held captive in Babylon and allowed them to return to Jerusalem.

"Cyrus declared each conquered area a province and asked that all provinces pay him a yearly sum of gold and silver. In return he promised to protect them from foreign invaders. This system worked out nicely for Cyrus, and he managed to build a wealthy empire."
"Did Cyrus build Persepolis?" Laurie asked, looking back at the photo.

"No, Persepolis was built by a king named Darius the Great, who ruled from 522 BC to 486 BC. Darius was called the Great because he continued to expand the empire’s borders, developed an organized system of rule, and improved the kingdom with major building projects. In order to stay informed about his empire, Darius needed people to travel and report back to him. So he built a great road, called the royal road, which connected the provinces. And this was way before the Romans built their famous roads, mind you. The royal road was useful for both transportation and communication.

"He also finished organizing the provinces—something that was begun during Cyrus’ time. And he appointed governors to manage each province. This way he could make sure each province paid him the right amount of gold and silver. But most famously Darius built a huge palace complex in Persepolis. This served as the center of government and a guest reception area. The plans for Persepolis—a city that aimed to impress all visitors with its riches and splendor—were so grand that Persepolis couldn’t be completed within Darius’ lifetime. It was actually finished by his son, the next king. There were palaces, great halls, a treasury, and more."

"But Grandpa, you wrote: ‘It is a shame that Alexander the Great laid waste to this magnificent city. I can only imagine what Persepolis might look like today, if only it had been preserved as a historic treasure,’" Laurie interrupted, reading from the journal. "I’m writing a report on Alexander the Great for homework. What did he do to Persepolis?"

"Well, the Persians and the Greeks eventually fought against each other. Clashes began during Darius’ time, continued through his son’s rule, and then finally, around 330 BC, the warrior Alexander the Great invaded and conquered Persia. When he reached Persepolis, he robbed the treasury, set fire to the palaces, and destroyed the sculptures—especially any that showed images of Persian kings. His conquests marked the end of the Persian Empire, and the dawn of the Greek.

"Laurie, have you heard of the Greek historian Herodotus? We know all this history because Herodotus traveled the Middle East collecting stories and recording information. He had a curious mind and a great interest in the actions and politics of humans. He wrote about the Persian Empire and Persian wars in a big book called The Histories . A great writer, he wrote as if he were telling someone a story face-to-face and often mixed in entertaining stories from his travels. I wish I could write such interesting histories," Grandpa said.
"But your history stories are just like that, Grandpa!" Laurie said. "They’re always interesting!"
"Thanks, Laurie." Grandpa smiled. "Maybe someday you can help me organize these journal entries. There’s a lot of history in here," he said, lightly tapping his journal.
"I’d be honored." Laurie grinned. "But for now I think I’m pretty busy with Alexander." She picked up the book and walked out of the study.
Laurie walked into Grandpa's study wearing a necklace and a long dress pinned at the shoulders. Her hair was gathered into a net. "How do I look, Grandpa? Can you guess what I am for Halloween?"
"A woman from ancient Greece of course!" Grandpa said, smiling. "And which city-state, may I ask, are you from?"
Laurie frowned. "I hadn't really thought about it. Sparta? Athens?" she answered, naming the only two old Greek cities she knew.
"Those are two very different cities. They were also enemies for many years. Maybe I should tell you about them so you can decide which one you'd rather live in.

"The Spartans were known for being serious, disciplined warriors. Every man joined the army and spent most of his life in the military. Training began at age seven, when boys were taken from their families and sent to live in military camps. They practiced sports for hours each day because having a weak body was considered dishonorable among Spartans. They were taught to live with only the barest necessities. Sometimes they were even starved on purpose so they would learn to fearlessly steal or kill their own food for survival. They were also served a black soup made of pork stewed in pigs' blood, vinegar, and salt to make them strong. Besides undergoing physical training, they had to learn how to become brave warriors. A good Spartan warrior could never cry out in pain or surrender easily.

"Even the Spartan women were expected to be strong and fearless. Unlike women in most other Greek cities, women of Sparta spent lots of time outdoors, exercising: they ran, did gymnastics, and danced. Part of a woman's duty was to provide her husband with a physically fit—preferably male—child who would become a strong warrior. In order to give birth to a healthy child, it was thought the mother must be fit and healthy too. Girls also received good educations and were allowed to own property as adults! This really shocked Greeks from other cities, where women weren't allowed such things.

"Spartan men and women were able to devote their lives to building a powerful Spartan military because all their farming and other labor was done by slaves. In fact, most of Sparta's economy ran on slave labor. But just because they had slaves doesn't mean Spartans were extravagant. They were expected to scorn wealth and luxury. They didn't have parties and, besides religious rites, had very few celebrations. They didn't wear jewelry or make much art. Today the word 'spartan' can describe someone who is courageous and self-disciplined, but also something that is extremely simple and not at all luxurious. What do you say, Laurie, could you be a Spartan?"
"Hmm . . . I could play sports, learn stuff, and eventually own my own house. That doesn't sound so bad, but I want to hear about Athens before I decide," Laurie said.

"You got it. Athenians enjoyed a lifestyle very different from the Spartans. Women's main duties were to raise children, take care of the household, and weave wool. If you were an Athenian, you probably would have made that beautiful dress of yours at home. Now taking care of the household could mean different things depending on how rich you were. If you were well-off, you probably had many slaves who would clean, watch the children, and bake bread. If you weren't, well, you might be doing all that work yourself. Although boys began school around age seven, Athenian girls didn't get to go to school. Around age 13 or so, they got married and began their lives as wives and mothers.

"But Athens was a truly incredible city. It is often called the birthplace of democracy because it was the first city to test out democracy, or government run by citizens. Athenians held city meetings at which all citizens—meaning Greek men who were born in the city—could share their opinions. Then citizens were allowed to vote. Sometimes they decided big issues, such as whether the city should go to war. Their style of government developed into the democracy we know today.

"Athens was also home to the famous Acropolis, an immense complex of temples, theaters, and other impressive buildings. The temples were dedicated to the worship of the Greeks' many gods and goddesses, whom the Athenians respected, feared, and often celebrated. Athenians were not spartan like the Spartans. They enjoyed sculpture, music, theater, poetry, and philosophy. Maybe you've heard of the great thinkers Socrates and Aristotle? They were both from Athens. Athenian citizens were deep thinkers, but they also liked wine, feasts, and celebrations! Grooming was also an important part of life; both men and women took hot baths and rubbed themselves with olive oil. Women owned lots of makeup and perfume. Athenians wore beautiful gold jewelry, a lot of which can be seen in museums today.

"Sparta and Athens had very different ideas about how people should live and govern themselves, but each grew to be a strong city. Eventually they clashed. Both wanted to rule the other Greek city-states, and in 431 BC, they fought in the Peloponnesian War. After nearly thirty years of battle, the Spartans were victorious and the good times in Athens ended.
"So what do you think, my little Grecian? Which ancient city would you like to live in—Sparta or Athens?" Grandpa asked.

Laurie considered her options. "Being a Spartan would mean I'd live a simple—and maybe harsh—life, but get to run around a lot. Being an Athenian would mean I'd witness the birth and development of democracy, but I wouldn't get to participate because I'm a girl. Sparta it is!" Laurie cried, snatching off her necklace and raising a fist in the air. She marched out of the study.
"Lace up your sneakers, Mom," she called. "We're jogging to the Halloween parade—in true Spartan style!"

6.title: Silk, Clay Soldiers, and a Great Wall

paragraphs.text: "Hey, Grandpa. What are these toy soldiers?" Laurie was looking through an archaeology book in Grandpa's study.

"Those aren't toys, Laurie," Grandpa said, looking at the picture. "Those are life-size clay soldiers! And they're on duty for eternity, guarding the tomb of the first emperor of one of the oldest civilizations in the world—China! Take a look at the next photo."

Laurie turned the page and saw an archaeologist carefully dusting the top of one clay soldier's head. The archaeologist and the statue were nearly the same size! "They are big!" she exclaimed. "And there are so many of them! Who was this emperor? He must have been really important to have all these soldiers made just for him."

"Well, as emperor, you can pretty much get whatever you want. But, yes, he was important. Known as Qin Shihuangdi, he was the first emperor of China and the emperor of the Qin dynasty, which lasted from 221 BC to 207 BC. In fact, the romanized name ‘China’ is believed to come from the Qin dynasty. Chinese civilization had been around since about 1600 BC, but Shihuangdi was the first ruler to unite the land into an empire ruled by one government. He was a cruel leader, but he did a lot for China. He ordered that the same measuring, writing, and money systems be used throughout the empire, which helped trade. He also organized the building of many roads, canals, and the longest structure ever built—the Great Wall of China."
"How was he cruel?" Laurie asked.

"Building these enormous projects, especially the Great Wall, required a lot of hard work. Shihuangdi forced his people to work for him. They often worked long hours on difficult jobs. Many actually died during the building of the Great Wall. He also believed that in order to rule a large empire, a ruler must make strict laws. One law punished scholars who thought or wrote about things the emperor believed were harmful or not useful to his empire. These included literature, philosophy, and of course criticism of his rule. He also famously burned all history books because he thought they might make people question his authority. Can you believe it?"
"Wow. Without history books how would we learn about the past?" Laurie asked.

"Well, written history helps, but there are other ways of discovering the past. Archaeology, for example! Luckily for Chinese historians, Shihuangdi's style of rule didn't last long. Soon after his death in 210 BC, his empire collapsed and the Han dynasty began.

"Han rulers looked to China's past for ideas about the future. They returned to the ideas of Confucius. He was an ancient scholar who believed that rulers should lead by good example only—not by forcing people to obey strict laws—and that people should respect their elders. His philosophy later spread throughout Asia, and his influence on Asian culture and society can still be seen today. Unlike the first emperor, Han rulers prized scholars. In fact, during the Han dynasty, a system was created to make sure that only the best scholars would receive government jobs. Anyone who wanted to work for the government had to take an extremely difficult test. China had the first government full of scholars! And nearly two thousand years later, this practice of making government employees pass tests was adopted by American and European governments too.

"The Han rulers continued to worry about foreign invaders, however, so they kept building Shihuangdi's Great Wall and created more roads for soldiers to travel on. With improved roads, trade continued to grow. The famous Silk Road, one of the greatest international trading routes in history, developed during the Han dynasty. Goods such as silk, tea, pottery, and spices traveled out of China to India, the Middle East, Russia, and Europe along that route. The exchange of ideas and culture between the East and the West also began along the Silk Road."
"Was the road made out of silk?" Laurie asked.

Grandpa chuckled. "No, but a lot of silk traveled along it. Silk, you see, was invented by the Chinese. Evidence shows they were making it as early as 1300 BC, but no one outside of China knew about it until centuries later. Once people of other countries touched the beautiful fabric, they loved it and wanted it for themselves. But the Chinese were determined to keep their silk-making process a secret. If foreigners wanted silk, they'd have to pay or trade. So silk was carried out of China along the Silk Road.

"Actually many things that were invented in ancient China would later travel to the West. There's paper, for one. And the wheelbarrow, the compass, and the first machine to detect earthquakes! The Han dynasty valued knowledge and learning, and they encouraged scientists to study and develop new things. They also valued the arts. The Han dynasty is known for its beautiful and unique pottery, poetry, and sculpture. Chinese civilization really flourished during this period. The dynasty lasted longer than any other—about four hundred years—and the Chinese consider it so important that even today they call themselves people of the Han."
"Laurie?" Mom suddenly called. "Have you seen my red silk blouse? I want to wear it when I go out tonight."
"You mean your Chinese red silk blouse?" Laurie shouted back.
"No, I don't have a Chinese blouse, Laurie." Now Mom's voice was coming from outside the door. "What are you guys talking about in there anyway?"

"Oh, all kinds of things! Silk, clay soldiers, a great wall!" Laurie answered. She turned to Grandpa and handed him back his book. "I'd better go help Mom find her blouse. Thanks again, Grandpa. See you in another place at another time!"
"Mom said you needed a cushion," Laurie said, walking into Grandpa's study. "I brought two just in case."

"Yes, I do need a cushion. Thank you," Grandpa said. He was sitting cross-legged on the floor. "I'm giving up chairs and devoting myself to deep thinking for one week. Maybe if I sit like Buddha and try to think like Buddha, I'll be able to write a great article on Buddha's life in ancient India." He picked up a small statue of the famous monk.
"Wait—Buddha was a real person?" Laurie asked, sitting down next to Grandpa.

"Yes. He was a real prince, named Siddhartha Gautama. He was born around the sixth century BC to the king and queen of the Shakya kingdom. Back then, the areas we know as India and Nepal were made up of small, independent kingdoms. Hinduism, which had been practiced in India for hundreds of years, divided society into four rigid classes, or castes. There were priests, royalty, merchants and farmers, and laborers. Since Siddhartha was born into a royal family, he enjoyed a life of luxury. His father wanted to protect his son from all the unpleasant things in the world, so he forbade Siddhartha from leaving the palace.

"But you know what happens when you tell people they can't do something. That becomes exactly what they want to do! So one day Siddhartha sneaked out of the palace. And he was shocked by what he saw: old people, sick people, and dead people! He saw great suffering and wondered why there was so much pain in the world. Then he met a hermit who said he had given up wealth to search for truth. Siddhartha decided he would do that too. So he left his kingdom and set out to lead a hermit's life.

"Siddhartha thought. And he fasted. And he walked. Then finally he sat beneath a tree by a river and thought very, very hard. After some time, he realized the truth about the world and why people suffer. It was under that tree that he became a buddha, or an 'enlightened one.' That means he truly understood the world." Grandpa closed his eyes and put his hands back over his knees. "Good story, eh?" he said. He sat very still.
"Yes, a very good story. But aren't you going to tell me what he found out? And what happened after that? Did he get up or sit there forever?" Laurie asked impatiently.

Grandpa looked at Laurie. "He didn't stay there forever. After he became enlightened, he set out to teach people what he had discovered, because he thought it would help them. He had discovered that people suffer because they have desires. They want things, and when they don't get them, they become upset or sad. In order to avoid suffering, people must get rid of their desires. This is what Buddha taught. He encouraged people to lead modest, moderate lives. He also encouraged them to ignore the Hindu caste system, because he believed that all people were equal. Hindus believed that only men in high castes could study religion. But Buddha said everyone was free to learn his teachings.

"Buddha had become enlightened in the powerful Magadha kingdom, which ruled northern India, and his story was famous there. The Magadha king, Bimbisara, invited Buddha to his palace. There Buddha taught King Bimbisara his knowledge of the world, and the king was so moved that he became a Buddhist. He offered one of his gardens to the wise Buddha. Siddhartha used the garden as a temporary home and teaching place. Many people learned about Buddhism there, and the popularity of his religion increased. He continued to teach until he died at age 80. By that time Buddhism was firmly established in India."
"What happened to Buddhism after he died?" Laurie asked.

"Even after his death, Buddhism continued to spread throughout India, especially thanks to King Ashoka of the great Mauryan kingdom. He was a vicious warrior and conqueror. During his rule, from about 270 BC to 232 BC, he attacked neighboring kingdoms and led wars to expand his territory, unifying much of India. After one particularly bloody war, however, he suddenly found himself horrified at his actions. He asked himself whether a violent life was worth living. Then he remembered the teachings of Buddha, which encouraged peace, equality, and harmony among all living things. Ashoka decided this was how people should live. He converted to Buddhism and declared his land a Buddhist kingdom. He wanted everyone to learn Buddha's teachings and live in harmony. Ashoka helped spread Buddhism throughout India, and for a while his kingdom flourished. But as you may guess, being peaceful only works if you can convince your neighbors and the next king to be peaceful too. After Ashoka's death political conflict and foreign invaders led to the end of the Mauryan kingdom and the end of a unified, peaceful India. In the years to come, Christians and Muslims would come from the west, forever changing Indian culture. Buddhism lost its power in India, but traveled north and east to take root in China, Korea, and Japan." Grandpa breathed deeply. "Now let's think about life, suffering, desire, peace, and enlightenment." He pointed to the extra cushion.
"Like this?" Laurie sat cross-legged, placed her hands over her knees, and closed her eyes.
"Exactly. That is how Siddhartha sat, and so shall we," Grandpa said, closing his eyes.
Laurie opened one eye to peek at Grandpa. He appeared to be deep in thought.
"Grandpa, it's pretty cool that you know all this stuff," she whispered. Then she closed her eyes and thought.
"Grandpa, you're home!" Laurie cried, running into Grandpa's study. "How was Italy?"
"Laurie! It was wonderful! I wish you could have gone too," Grandpa said. "I studied many artifacts from ancient Rome that I had never seen before."
"Did you bring anything back to show me? A toga?" Laurie asked.
Grandpa laughed. "Unfortunately I couldn't bring home any togas. But I did put together a slide show!"
Grandpa switched off the lights and turned on the projector.
"Ooh, is that Julius Caesar?" Laurie asked, looking at a picture of a statue.
"No, but you're close! This is Octavian, Caesar's grandnephew, who came to power after Caesar was murdered. He's more commonly known as Augustus, the first emperor of Rome."
"Wait—if he was the first emperor, who was Julius Caesar?" Laurie asked.

"Hmm . . . Maybe we should start from the beginning. According to legend, long ago two brothers named Romulus and Remus were left in a basket on the Tiber River in present-day Italy. A wolf saved the baby boys and fed them. Then a shepherd and his wife found the boys and raised them as their own. The two brothers grew up to be brave and strong. One day they decided to build a city. But they got into a fight. Romulus killed his brother, named the city ‘Rome' after himself, and became the first king. This was in 753 BC.

"A series of kings continued to rule Rome for the next 250 years or so. But eventually Romans grew to dislike kings, because they thought kings gave themselves too much power. Instead they formed a government run by the people, or the public, so Rome became a republic. Julius Caesar was the last leader of the republic. When that system collapsed, Augustus began a new style of rule and became the first emperor of the new Roman Empire.

"Augustus was a great commander who led Rome into an age of cultural and geographical expansion. The name of the month August comes from his name, which means the great one. People liked him because during his rule Roman civil wars finally ended. A long period of peace began, and the Roman Empire grew into the most powerful empire in the world. It included not only modern-day Italy, but England, France, Germany, Egypt, and Turkey as well."
A new slide appeared. "Ha-ha! Grandpa, is that you in a scuba suit?" Laurie said.

"It is! I was diving for artifacts. Many Roman remains have been found underwater! This is because the Romans traded mainly by sea. They built great ships and sailed from ports near Rome to other cities in Europe, as well as to Africa and the Middle East. But not all journeys were successful. Sunken ships full of trade items have become valuable resources for people studying ancient Rome. For example, these pots were discovered aboard a sunken ship. We now know they were used to carry olive oil, sauces, and wine for trade."
"Hey, what's that?" Laurie asked, pointing at the next slide. It looked like a picture of an old pool. "It's pretty."

"Those are the ruins of a bathhouse. Bathhouses were cheap and very popular in ancient Rome. Nearly everyone went. Just like today's spas, Roman bathhouses had hot tubs, steam rooms, saunas, and cold pools to plunge into before or after your bath! The bathhouse wasn't just somewhere to bathe. It was also a place for families and friends to go and relax.

"Another popular place in Roman cities was the forum. It was like the downtown area in a modern city. Besides being a center for politics, the forum was usually a major shopping center! There you could walk along rows of merchants and craftsmen selling pottery, jewelry, spices, and wine. And if you got hungry, you could purchase some fast food—maybe olives, beans, and bread—from a food stand. These are the walls of a market near the forum in ancient Rome. The Romans were great builders, so many remains are still in good condition.

"But even though we'll never be able to see exactly how the Romans lived, we hear the ancient Romans every day—in our languages! Their language, Latin, isn't spoken much anymore. But it is the root language for many European languages. We call them Romance languages because of their connection to Rome. Many English words come from Latin as well. So even if you don't know Latin, if you know English or a Romance language, you can probably figure out what many words mean. For example, our word 'history' comes from the Latin word historia !

"Our language owes a lot to Roman gods and goddesses too. Romans thought the gods lived near the heavens, and they believed the movements of the stars were gods traveling across the sky. This is why many of our planets are named after gods and goddesses! Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, Neptune, and Saturn were all mighty gods. And Venus was the goddess of love and beauty."
"Laurie, we have to leave," Laurie heard Dad call from downstairs. "You'll be late for your violin lesson!"
"Uh-oh. Time to go. Thanks, Grandpa. Those were interesting photos," Laurie said.

"Wait . . . it's not a toga, but I have something for you." Grandpa pulled a ring from his pocket. "A ring with your initials on it. And 2010 in Roman numerals on the inside," he said, "so you'll always remember when I gave it to you."
"Oh, thank you! I love it!" Laurie put the ring on and gave Grandpa a hug.
"Now, go! Don't keep your dad waiting." He smiled.
"Bye, Grandpa!"

Laurie burst into Grandpa's study, blowing on a paper noisemaker. "Grandpa, will you come downstairs to watch the countdown with us?" It was New Year's Eve, and Grandpa had been in his study since after dinner.
"Of course! Is it that time already?" Grandpa said.
"Yep. It's almost 2011!" Laurie looked at the calendar hanging on the wall. "You need a new calendar!"
"I always find it amazing that humans have been on Earth for well over ten thousand years, but our calendar only says 2011!" Grandpa said.
"What year is it really?" Laurie asked, confused.

"It depends on when you start your calendar. Most of the world uses a calendar that begins with the birth of Jesus Christ. Every year before that is marked with 'BC,' which stands for before Christ. Every year after that is marked by 'AD,' which stands for the Latin words anno Domini , meaning in the year of the Lord. Before Jesus, most calendars were based on the cycles of the moon or the sun, or both. It was also common to count years based on the start of a leader's or dynasty's rule. But Jesus changed the world. In the sixth century, a monk created a calendar that began with the birth of Jesus."
"So the birth of one man changed the way humans record time?" Laurie asked.
"Yes. And not only that. His life and death also gave rise to the largest religion in the world—Christianity."
"I only know a little about Jesus from the stories around Christmas time." Laurie glanced at the clock. It was 11:46 p.m. "What was so special about his life?"

"I'll tell you as much as I can—but quickly, because I know Mom and Dad are waiting for us. Jesus was born in Bethlehem, a Jewish city that was part of the Roman Empire. He was the son of a carpenter named Joseph and a woman named Mary, who raised him in the Jewish tradition. Many people believed he was the leader who would free the Jews from Roman rule. Others thought he was the son of God. Anyway, Jesus studied Judaism carefully and became a preacher. He preached about love, heaven, and the forgiveness of sins. He wanted to tell people everywhere that God loved them.

"Now, although Jesus worshipped the same god as the Jews, his teachings strayed from traditional Jewish beliefs. So some Jews accepted him, but many others did not. And the Romans didn't bother him, because they generally allowed their subjects to follow different religions as long as no one harmed the state. As Jesus gained more and more followers, however, many Jews and Romans began to worry about his power. When Jesus was just 33 years old, a Roman official ordered him to be killed.

"But even after his death, Jesus' followers kept believing in what he had said, and Christianity arose. At first this religion was practiced by only a small number of people, and not many others understood it. But as Jesus' followers journeyed to tell others about their new faith, Christianity spread throughout the Mediterranean world.

"These early Christians weren't treated very well in the Roman Empire. Roman emperors often held ceremonies related to Roman gods and goddesses. They wanted all their people to participate. But Christians believed in a single god and wouldn't take part in anything related to Roman gods. So some Roman leaders saw Christians as a threat because they obeyed their faith rather than the Roman emperor. These Romans persecuted Christians. But Christianity continued to gain popularity because it gave people hope. Christians spoke of life after death, when people would live in the kingdom of God. They also said that all people were equal before God. This included everyone—from emperors to commoners."
"So I guess common people liked the religion, but the emperors didn't?" Laurie asked.

"Right. Not at first anyway. But in 312 AD, the Roman emperor Constantine converted to Christianity, and persecution of the Christians ended. In 380 Emperor Theodosius made Christianity the empire's official religion, creating the world's first Christian empire. Gradually Christians began settling in large communities and building churches. Bishops, who were the heads of churches, became more powerful. In big cities, such as Rome, their authority extended from religion into politics.

"Once Christianity gained the approval of Roman emperors, it grew and grew within the empire. Churches were built using state money. Courts run by churches appeared, and they soon held more power than the Roman government over religious issues. The bishops of Rome, known as popes, became especially influential. They claimed authority over all other churches. At the same time, the Roman Empire was being attacked by nomadic troops from Europe and Asia. As the state grew weaker and Christianity grew stronger, people found more security with the church than they did with the state.

"Soon Christianity spread beyond the Roman Empire. Part of Jesus' message was that God was universal, so Christians believed they should spread Jesus' teachings throughout the world. Roman roads and access to the Mediterranean Sea made it easy for Christians to go on missions. Christians moved north throughout Europe and converted the people there. By the time the Roman Empire reached its last days around 500 AD, Christianity had become the dominant religion in Europe. And that brings us to the eve of the Middle Ages, Laurie, when the Christian church and the pope became the supreme authority on nearly everything."

"The eve of the Middle Ages? Grandpa, it's the eve of 2011 and here we are sitting and talking about stuff that happened over 1,500 years ago! Let's go downstairs and celebrate what's happening now!" Laurie grabbed Grandpa's hand.
"Okay. You have a point," Grandpa said, standing up. "I should stop rambling."
"Happy 2011, anno Domini !" Laurie cried as they walked out of the study together.

Laurie was lying on the floor of Grandpa’s study one rainy afternoon, doing her homework. She saw a crumpled piece of paper near the trash can and smoothed it out. "Hey, Grandpa, what’s this? Did you draw it?" she asked, looking at a drawing of a vicious-looking man on a horse.
"That is the work of a talented student, not me. He found it more entertaining to draw Attila the Hun than to listen to my lecture on Hun artifacts," Grandpa said.
"Attila the Hun? I’ve heard of him! Wasn’t he a horrible villain?" Laurie asked.

"Well, it depends on who you ask," Grandpa said, joining Laurie on the floor. "The Huns were a group of nomadic horsemen who lived on the steppes of western central Asia. Most of what we know about them was written down by men of the Roman Empire—the empire the Huns invaded. Since the Huns had no written history of their own, it is difficult for historians to explain their past. But we know they lived in big tents made of wooden frames covered in wool. And they moved around when the seasons changed to find new grazing land for their large herds of cattle, sheep, and horses, which they depended on for food. And we know that they had a big impact on the Roman Empire." Laurie heard a rumble of thunder and looked outside. The sky had grown dark.

"Meanwhile the Romans lived in busy cities. They were developing governments, conquering neighboring lands, and organizing taxes. Imagine what they must have thought when they encountered the Huns! They couldn’t understand their language or way of life. So they called these very different people barbarians, which is actually what they called anyone who was not from Rome."
"When I eat with my hands, Mom says, ‘Stop acting like a barbarian!’" Laurie said. "She just doesn’t understand my way of eating!"

"Exactly!" Grandpa laughed. "But don’t tell your mother I said that. Anyway, back to the Huns. They were the greatest horsemen in the world at the time. Old tales say that Hun children were taught to ride horses soon after they learned to walk. By the time they were adults, they were fast, skilled riders. They had to be, because horses were their main means of transportation. Hun warriors also fought on horseback. They would race into villages, firing arrows, looking larger than life, and terrifying the villagers. It is said that Hun warriors cut and scarred their faces in order to make themselves look more frightening!"
Laurie jumped as a bright flash of lightning lit the sky, followed by a clap of thunder.

"Around the fourth century, the Huns began moving west—like a dark storm cloud—raining terror on everything in their path. Maybe they needed more land for their herds or maybe they were driven away by the strong walls China had built to keep them off Chinese territory. The important thing is that when the Huns moved west, they forced other barbarians off their land. So then these other barbarian tribes had to move farther west. They moved into the Roman Empire, upsetting cities there. Some tribes became part of the Roman Empire. Some lived right on the borders. And others just caused trouble.

"The Visigoths, one powerful tribe, were farmers who needed land to grow crops. After fighting Roman armies for some years, they settled within the empire. In exchange for land and peace, they defended the empire’s borders. But the Visigoths soon grew unhappy because the Romans didn’t give them everything they had promised. In the fourth century, the fearless Visigoth leader named Alaric led his soldiers into cities in what is now Italy and Greece. The Visigoths invaded, stole what they wanted, and left. This is called sacking. In 410 AD the Visigoths sacked Rome. It was a huge shock to the Romans, and many feared it would be the end of the greatest empire in the world."
"Was it?" asked Laurie.

"No. The Roman Empire held on for a while longer, and the barbarian invasions continued. The next major attack was from the Huns." Grandpa took something out of his pocket and tossed it to Laurie. "Heads up!"
She opened her palm and saw it was a coin.

"In the fifth century, Attila the Hun—the man on that coin you’re holding—rose to power. He gathered thousands of Hun warriors and led them into southeastern Europe. After he conquered those lands, he moved his armies into Roman territories in modern-day Poland, Hungary, and Germany. The Huns became wealthy by looting cities, but also by taking prisoners and selling them. And they made money from peace treaties. These treaties often required the Romans to pay large amounts of money to the Huns. One treaty demanded nine hundred kilograms of gold a year!"
"So what happened? Did the Huns become the richest, most powerful people in the world?" Laurie asked.

"They didn’t, although it seemed possible at one point. Attila the Hun died in 453 AD. He died of something silly—a nosebleed, they say—on his wedding night. How sad for a warrior who had survived so many battles. Shortly after that a civil war broke out among the Huns, destroying their empire. But the damage they and the other barbarians had done to the Roman Empire had weakened it forever. It, too, soon collapsed. The different regions created new governments and boundaries. Slowly Europe as we know it began to take shape."
Lightning flashed, thunder boomed, and suddenly the lights went out.

"Ahh!" Laurie shrieked. Grandpa reached for a candle by the window and lit it. "Here I am, Laurie." He put his arm around his granddaughter. "And if a scar-faced barbarian comes crashing through that door, don’t worry—I’ll protect you!" He held the candle up like a torch.
"Grandpa!" Laurie giggled.
"Laurie? Grandpa? Are you guys okay up there?" Dad shouted from downstairs.
"We’re okay, Dad! Safe and sound," Laurie answered.
"Grandpa! I got a starring role in the class play!" Laurie bounded into Grandpa's study.
"That's terrific!" Grandpa said, giving her a hug. "Tell me more."
"The title of the play is Medieval Nights , but our teacher says it's based on some book called The Canterbury Tales ."
"Ah! That's one of the most famous books of the Middle Ages. It was written by a man named Geoffrey Chaucer," Grandpa said.
"The play is about a group of travelers going to visit a cathedral. I'm an English queen who meets a knight and sends him on a long journey!"
Grandpa smiled. "Then I'm sure you live in a magnificent castle! How much do you know about cathedrals, knights, and castles?" he asked.
"Not much," Laurie admitted. "My class is going to study the Middle Ages next week."
"I could give you an introduction," Grandpa offered.
"Sure." Laurie settled down on the couch.

"The Middle Ages refers to the time between the collapse of the Roman Empire and the beginning of the European Renaissance, so from around the fifth century to the fifteenth century. In Europe the Christian Church had become the richest, most powerful institution. You, Queen Laurie, might have been baptized in a cathedral, like the one in your play. You'd attend church every Sunday, get married in a church, pay taxes to the church, and go there to seek advice and make confessions.

"Church buildings became really beautiful during the Middle Ages. Medieval architects designed tall buildings with pointy steeples that reached toward heaven. The insides were filled with expensive sculptures, golden goblets, and other fancy things. Huge, stained-glass windows flooded the church with colored light. But these beautiful windows weren't just decoration—they also told stories. Many people those days couldn't read, so how could they learn the stories of the Bible? Well, priests could tell them of course. But people could also look up at the massive windows and see the story of Jesus, for example, pictured in the glass."
"Wow . . . Like a storybook." Laurie gazed at the windows in the study, trying to imagine a story painted there.
"I bet there is a monk and a nun in your play too," Grandpa said.
"Yep. But I'm glad I get to be the queen and wear a nice costume," Laurie confessed. "The nun just wears a boring gown and something to cover her head."

"Men and women who became monks and nuns devoted their lives to the church. They didn't have time to worry about things like pretty clothes. They lived in their own communities, separated from the town. Monks wore plain, brown robes, ate simple food, and spent their days praying and studying the Bible. They were often well-educated and could read and write. Many copied out long sections of the Bible in beautiful script. Nuns devoted most of their day to prayer too, but they were busy with chores such as cooking, cleaning, and sewing.

"Many medieval Christians wanted to create an entirely Christian world. But there were still strong empires with different religions. For example, the Muslim Abbasid Empire ruled northern Africa and the Middle East. European Christians didn't like that their holy land—including Jerusalem, where Christianity developed—was controlled by Muslims. Many Christians journeyed to these places to worship. And church leaders worried about Christians' safety because sometimes they were attacked. So the pope asked barons—wealthy landowners—to gather their armies and fight for Christianity. These battles, known as the Crusades, lasted for nearly two hundred years and killed almost nine million people. The Christian fighters were called Crusaders and wore red crosses on their armor. Many were knights. Is the knight in your play a Crusader, Laurie?" Grandpa asked.
"I don't know! All I know is that he travels around and when he finally returns, he gets married and lives in a castle," Laurie said.
"Is he chivalrous and handsome?" Grandpa asked, smiling.
"Handsome? No! Yuck," Laurie answered, crinkling her nose. "And I don't know what chivalrous means."

"Chivalrous means good, honorable, and polite to women. All knights were expected to be chivalrous. They practiced this, along with fighting skills, from a young age. Knights worked for barons. In exchange for protection, barons gave their knights some land and maybe a nice castle to live in. Battles were often deadly, so knights were respected for their bravery. Plus they made an awe-inspiring sight when they dressed for battle. In the early Middle Ages, a knight's armor was a suit made of tiny iron rings linked together. But eventually knights realized they needed more protection and began wearing suits made of iron and steel plates. It was like having a full-body shield that weighed over 22 kilograms!"
"I'd rather hear about the castles," Laurie requested. "Since I'll be living in one."

"Of course. Castles were large, sturdy stone buildings with many rooms. There were great candlelit halls for feasts and celebrations, but also dark, damp prisons. Castles had to protect the owner, as well as the servants, guards, and entertainers who lived there. Neighboring noblemen often fought each other for land. So many castles had stone defense walls that circled the entire castle. Sometimes there were even two or three walls. Guards would stand on top of the walls and shoot arrows or throw huge rocks at intruders. Many castles also had a moat, which was a man-made canal around the castle. In order to cross it, visitors needed to have a bridge let down, or else swim across. The tall towers were often lookout points to spot intruders. Or perhaps to spot a knight returning from his journey!"
"Laurie! Will you help me make dinner?" Laurie's mom called from downstairs.

"Coming, Mom!" Laurie hollered back. Then she giggled. "Silly Mom. Queens don't cook dinner!" She turned to Grandpa and raised her chin like a queen. "Be sure to join us for our feast in the great hall tonight."
Bowing slightly, Grandpa answered, "It would be my pleasure, Your Highness."
"Laurie, I got you something to celebrate your first horseback riding lesson," Grandpa announced, meeting Laurie at the top of the stairs. "Mongolian boots!"
"Wow! They're pretty. But why Mongolian?" Laurie said, holding up the decorative orange and turquoise boots.

"Because the Mongols have a history of being excellent horse riders! Back in the 1200s, when their empire was the mightiest in the world, they had riding skills even your instructor would envy. They could eat, sleep, and pick up an arrow from the ground without ever getting off their horses!"
Laurie raised her eyebrows.
"Not only that, but they have an amazing history too," Grandpa continued. "Would you like to hear a bit?"
"Okay," Laurie answered.
"Come on in," he said, and Laurie followed him into the study.

"Mongolia," Grandpa began, "is a country in Asia, between Russia and China. Its land is a mix of mountains, grasslands, and the driest desert in the world. Because Mongols live in such rough environments, they have become pretty tough themselves. But they love their land and feel deeply connected to it. The Mongols, you know, believe their people were created when a blue wolf and a female deer traveled to a sacred mountain in Mongolia. There the two animals mated and the deer later gave birth to a human. This human was the first ancestor of the Mongols." Grandpa paused to lift a furry hat off the bookshelf and place it on his head.

"The early Mongols," he continued, "were nomads who lived in tents and migrated seasonally with their large herds of sheep, camels, yaks, and horses. In summer they lived in the high steppes. In winter they traveled to warmer, lower lands, in search of new grass for their animals. To the Mongols, land was sacred, so they would not plow it or settle on it. Water was sacred, so they would not bathe in it or dirty it with any of their waste. And the sky was sacred, so they climbed to the tops of mountains to be closer to their greatest god, known as Eternal Blue Heaven.

"For many years the Mongols existed as separate tribes. Even though the Mongol tribes shared a common culture and way of life, they fought often. At one point the fighting was so intense, it looked like they might all destroy each other. But then in the twelfth century, a great leader united them. He built a mighty empire that connected the East and the West forever."
"Who?" Laurie blurted out. "Was he a Mongol?"

"Yes. He was a Mongol named Temujin. According to legend, he was born holding a blood clot in his fist. This was either a sign of danger or a sign that he would be a great warrior. Temujin turned out to be a strong, brave warrior. After many battles he became the khan, or leader, of his tribe. Once he had conquered all the neighboring tribes, he was called Genghis Khan, which means oceanic or universal leader. Under Genghis Khan's leadership, the Mongol Empire expanded to include most of Asia, much of the Middle East, and a large part of modern-day Russia. It was the largest empire ever established by one man."
"Wow. Really?" Laurie remarked. "What made him such a great leader?"

"Well, Genghis Khan understood what is needed to keep a stable empire: a common written language, law and order, good communication, and a strong, loyal army. He made sure the Mongols had all these things. The Mongols never had a written language, so he chose the alphabet of one of the conquered tribes and made it the official Mongolian script. Then he ordered the Mongolian cultural and social rules to be written in a book and demanded that people be punished if they disobeyed them. And—at a time when there were no postal systems—he built a messenger system that could quickly carry messages on horseback across long distances. But perhaps his greatest ideas had to do with the army. He separated soldiers from their fellow tribesmen so that they would be more loyal to him than to their fellow soldiers. And he promoted them based on their skill rather than their social position. This was a revolutionary idea at the time.

"Genghis Khan also had the reputation of being one of his people. That means he wore the same clothes they wore, ate the same food they ate, and rode the same horses they rode. He didn't treat himself like a king or an emperor. This made him popular. When he died in 1227, a great funeral was held for him. He was buried at the mountain where the blue wolf and the deer created the first Mongol so many years ago. But the exact location has never been found because after the funeral, eight hundred horsemen rode over the spot to destroy any sign of a grave."
"Whoa . . . Eight hundred horseback riders?" Laurie asked.

"Well, important men get impressive funerals, and Genghis Khan was a very important Mongol. Under his leadership, the Mongol Empire left a huge impact on the world. After being abandoned for some time, the Silk Road reopened under Genghis Khan's rule. The Mongols helped promote the transfer of goods, ideas, and culture between Asia and Europe. The Silk Road brought so many interesting items from the East to the West that Westerners became extremely curious about Asia. In the late thirteenth century, the famous Italian explorer Marco Polo traveled to China. He lived in the palace of Kublai Khan, Genghis Khan's grandson who had become the emperor of China. Marco Polo's adventures inspired Christopher Columbus to sail around the world in search of a faster route to Asia. I'd say the Mongol Empire was pretty important, wouldn't you?"
"Yes." Laurie pulled on the boots. "But more importantly, these boots are beautiful. I hope Mom lets me wear them to school. Thanks, Grandpa! Giddyap!" she cried, galloping out of the study.
"Laurie, come take a look at this." Grandpa was reading the newspaper at his desk. "There's going to be a Renaissance fair in Buck County. Do you want to go?"
"What's a Renaissance fair?" Laurie asked, looking up from her book.

"A Renaissance fair," Grandpa began reading from the newspaper ad, "is a place to see, hear, and taste life as it was during Elizabethan England." He looked at Laurie. "That means the time when Queen Elizabeth was on the throne, from 1558 to 1603. It was the height of the English Renaissance. There will probably be a market, performances, and actors."
"What does renaissance mean?" Laurie asked.

"Aren't you taking French at school?" Grandpa said teasingly. "Renaissance means rebirth in French. We call the period of European history from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century the Renaissance because all of Europe changed dramatically during this time. There was a rebirth in art, education, government, and religion. It was also a time of great discovery in both the sciences and geography.

"The Renaissance began in Florence, Italy, in the 1300s. Florence was a big trading city because it was located neatly between the Middle East, Europe, and Asia. Many merchants, who used to be part of the lower class, became wealthy. This was the beginning of the middle class. They weren't nobles or royalty, and they didn't have any fancy titles to their names, but they had money to spend freely. They also had free time to think, read, and enjoy life. Many scholars think this brought about a renewed interest in art and learning.

"The middle class wanted to spend their wealth on art, books, and music. Wealthy families gave money to artists and asked them to make paintings and sculptures for the city. Many of these artists are still admired today. Let's see, I'm sure I have a book around here somewhere . . ." Grandpa stood up and examined his bookshelf. "Aha! Artists of the Italian Renaissance ," he read, pulling the title from the shelf. "I'm sure you'll recognize a lot of stuff in here."
Laurie flipped through the pages. "The Mona Lisa !" she exclaimed.
"Right! The Mona Lisa was painted by Leonardo da Vinci in the early 1500s."
Laurie turned the page. "Oh! He's naked!" she cried.

"That's Michelangelo's famous sculpture David ," Grandpa answered. "During the Renaissance, artists began learning how to create more realistic images of humans. They studied the human body carefully, and tried to draw and sculpt what they saw. It was really a revolution in art.

"Education in Europe also developed and changed during the Renaissance. In the Middle Ages, people learned to read and write so they could study and copy the Bible. But people of the Renaissance wanted to study books from classical Greece and Rome. This was called new learning or humanism."
"Humanism?" Laurie echoed. "That's a funny word. Were they studying humans?"

"Well, yes!" Grandpa answered. "People were curious about what human beings could do with science, art, philosophy—everything! They believed that humans had skills, and that these skills could be developed to perfection. What's one of your skills, Laurie?" Grandpa asked.
"Um, I always get As in reading," Laurie replied.

"So you would have been encouraged to develop that talent by reading classic Greek and Roman books. Unfortunately this would only have been encouraged if you were a boy. Girls received just basic education and then learned to cook and sew at home. Rather than going to a university at age 15, like boys did, girls would probably get married to an older man and start a family."
"That's not fair." Laurie frowned.

"No, it's not. But many things came out of the Renaissance that everybody, including women, could appreciate later. One of the greatest inventions was the printing press, which was created in Germany in 1440. Thanks to the printing press, books didn't have to be copied by hand anymore. So they were cheaper and more people could buy them. Libraries were built and regular people, not just nobles or clergymen, learned how to read. The printing press changed European—no, human—society forever! Can you imagine a world without books, Laurie?"
Laurie shook her head forcefully. "No way!"

"Many things were invented during the Renaissance. Have you heard of the Italian Galileo Galilei? Human eyes saw the surface of the moon for the first time with his telescope. He was also influential in getting people to accept the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, and not the other way around."
"Of course the Earth moves around the sun! Even I know that and I'm only in fourth grade." Laurie giggled. "Will we see Galileo's telescope at the fair?" she asked.

"No. Galileo was Italian and we're going to an English fair, remember? The Renaissance began in Italy, but later it spread to England, France, Germany, and all of Europe. We'll probably see actors playing famous people of the English Renaissance, like the writer William Shakespeare. Or Sir John Harington, inventor of the flushing toilet—another great invention of the Renaissance! And at the market I bet we'll see barrel makers, blacksmiths, and milliners."
"Millionaires!" Laurie said, surprised.

"No—milliners! They make hats," Grandpa answered with a chuckle. "Hats and wigs were in fashion back then. In fact, anyone over age 12 was required to wear a hat. During the Renaissance, clothing was a symbol of wealth and class—by law. For example, nobody except the queen was allowed to wear purple. And peasants weren't allowed to wear pink or gold-colored fabric!"
"That's crazy!" Laurie cried. She looked down at her own clothes. "What are we going to wear to the fair?"
"Well, we could go in our regular clothes. But it would be fun to get dressed up, wouldn't it?" Grandpa grinned. He grabbed a long black feather from his desk and stuck it behind her ear.
Laurie's eyes shined. "Yeah, it would! I can't wait."

Laurie heard the beating of a drum coming from the study. Then she heard Grandpa call out, "Hear me, people, for I speak the truth! Tell this story to your children so the name Sundiata—the Lion King—lives forever!"
"Grandpa!" Laurie pushed the study door open. "What are you doing?"

Grandpa sat on the couch with a large drum. A stringed instrument was by his feet. "I'm practicing for my African storytelling performance. Hayside Elementary asked me to give a presentation to their third grade. I'll be telling them about the golden age of Africa."
"But what are the instruments for?" Laurie asked.
"African storytellers play instruments while sharing their legends and histories. It's usually this instrument called the kora and maybe a drum."
"That's cool. What's the story about?" Laurie asked.

"It's about three kingdoms of Africa—the Ghana, Mali, and Songhai kingdoms. These developed on the edge of the Sahara Desert. During the Middle Ages, some of the richest kingdoms in the world developed there. Originally, people of the Sahara were desert nomads who wandered from oasis to oasis to find water and vegetation for themselves and their herds. But legend says they always returned to one oasis, where they left their heavy belongings with a woman named Buktu. Eventually this spot became a city called Timbuktu, named after the woman. By around 1100 AD, Timbuktu was a major city along the trading route that crossed the Sahara and carried goods from Africa to Arabia."
"Isn't the Sahara Desert huge?" Laurie asked. "How did they cross it?"

"It is huge. Imagine that you have to journey through it for days and nights carrying loads of gold, fabric, iron tools, and clay pots. What would you do?" Grandpa paused and looked at Laurie. "Gather up your camels, of course! The Africans traveled by camel caravan. These animals can walk through hot sand for days without food or water. So traders loaded up about a hundred camels with goods and then set off into the desert. Usually the trip to Arabia took about forty days.
"Can you guess what made the Africans so rich during their golden age?" Grandpa asked with a smile.
"Gold!" Laurie responded.

"Right! Gold and . . . salt," Grandpa said. "Salt was so important back then that it had the same value as gold. Salt is used to keep food from spoiling. It also makes food taste good. But most importantly it is essential to human bodies. We can't live without salt! And when you sweat, you lose a lot of salt, so it was especially important to Africans who lived in a hot climate and sweated a lot every day.

"Salt and gold helped the first great African kingdom—the Ghana kingdom—come to power. Ghana's cities became home to the best artists and scholars on the continent. But eventually the Ghanaians were overrun by a group of Islamic Arabs. Wars broke out as different groups tried to gain control over the cities. Then a brave warrior named Sundiata, or 'hungering lion,' led his people to defeat the existing rulers. In 1235 he established the next great kingdom—the Mali kingdom—and created a stable government with a tax system. Under his rule, Mali grew richer and stronger every year. Then in 1307 another great leader, named Mansa Musa, came to the throne. He doubled the size of the kingdom and tripled its trade. Gold was flowing from Mali to Arabia, and then into Europe.

"Islamic Arabic traders had been trying to convert Africans to Islam for years, and Mali was the first kingdom to accept Islam as its religion. In 1324 Mansa Musa, a devoted Muslim, made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca, the birthplace of Islam. This pilgrimage gave Arabs their first image of how rich Mali was. Mansa Musa's caravan was the largest ever to travel across the Sahara. Five-hundred slaves walked before the great king. Mansa Musa, with his party of over fifty-thousand people, followed. One-hundred camels walked behind them, carrying over thirty-thousand pounds of gold. Mansa Musa was proud to present the riches of his kingdom to the Arabs. Everywhere he went he gave out beautiful gifts. He also went to markets and bought everything the merchants offered him. And he always paid in pure gold. Mansa Musa left quite an impression in Arabia. News of his incredible pilgrimage even traveled to Europe, where people were stunned by this rich king of Africa."
"Did it make Europeans want to go to Africa too?" Laurie asked.

"It did. But we'll get to that later. Still one more great African kingdom arose after Mali—the Songhai kingdom. Songhai was a territory that had been captured by Mali, and its people wanted their freedom back. In 1468 a Songhai leader named Sunni Ali Ber took over Timbuktu and gained control of the Saharan trading routes. The Mali kingdom fell apart, and the Songhai kingdom ruled West Africa.

"But no golden age lasts forever. In 1591 Muslims from Morocco attacked the Songhai kingdom. And you were absolutely right, Laurie. Learning about the rich African kingdoms made people want to take control of Africa. In the 1600s the Portuguese and Dutch began setting up their own cities and colonies there. But that's another story."
"Wow, I never knew Africa had kingdoms like that," Laurie said.

"Yeah," Grandpa said sadly. "Most people only learn about the slave trade that brought Africans to the Americas. But Africans have a much greater history to be proud of. And I will be proud to tell it." Grandpa tapped his drum.

"Well, I have a great story of my own to tell." Laurie moved the drum between her legs and tapped it. "Listen to my story. Here are the adventures of a fourth-grader!" And she began to tell Grandpa about a brave young girl named Laurie and her wise grandfather who studied the past.

When Laurie got home from school, she ran straight to the mailbox. Grandpa had gone to the Southwest a week ago but hadn't sent her anything yet. Had he forgotten about her? She saw a postcard and a yellow envelope addressed to her. "Finally!" she thought.

Hi, Laurie! How's my favorite granddaughter? I made it to New Mexico. I'm in Chaco Culture National Historical Park studying the ancient Pueblos—Native Americans who lived in the Southwest over 1,500 years ago.
