Many different peoples lived here, but as a group, we call them the Pueblos, after the houses they built. Their houses had connecting walls and rooms built on top of one another. They were really more like villages than individual houses.

The biggest Pueblo settlements are found here in Chaco Canyon. We archaeologists call them the great houses. One house, Pueblo Bonito, covered about three acres, and probably housed about twelve hundred people. Pueblo society had no leaders, so living together took a lot of organization and patience. But amazingly, they were one of the most peaceful people this country has ever known. I'll write you a letter explaining more when I set up camp tonight. But I had to send you a postcard of the amazing Pueblo Bonito!

Laurie examined the image on the postcard. All the walls really were connected! She tried to imagine living in a house that was connected to everybody else's. It would be strange to live so close to her classmates and teacher!

She wished she could have gone with Grandpa to see the ancient sites. There were so many things she wanted to know. If the Pueblos moved into the Southwest 1,500 years ago, where were they before that? Where were they now? She opened the envelope and started reading Grandpa's letter.
Dear Laurie,
I know you wish you were here and I do too. I bet you also have lots of questions about the Pueblos. So let's start at the beginning.

Native Americans had been living in the United States for thousands of years before the Europeans arrived and colonized the land. Many historians think the natives originally came from Asia and arrived in North America during the Ice Age. Back then a land bridge connected Asia to Alaska. Native Americans might have crossed this land bridge while following bison and other large mammals they hunted. But Pueblos have their own version of how they got here. They believe they came from the earth, in a holy place underground, and were then led to the surface by a god.

Origins aside, we know for sure that the first Pueblos were nomadic hunters and gatherers. Eventually they began building pit houses. These were circular underground houses, dug five or six feet into the ground. Around the year 700, they began building aboveground, but kept underground rooms for special religious ceremonies. Now their houses were made of stone and red-clay bricks, but still had no doors or windows. So how did the Pueblos get in and out of their houses? Through the roof! They climbed up a wooden ladder to the top of the wall, and then down another ladder to enter their homes. Imagine you're returning home after a hunt, carrying a large deer over your back. Or you're coming back from the spring with two large jugs full of water! You would become a very skilled ladder climber!

Maybe you'd like to know a little more about the Pueblos' daily life. They worked very hard. Women ground corn and gathered seeds, berries, and nuts for the family meals. They also made pottery. Men took care of the crops, went on hunts, and wove baskets and blankets. Young children and girls stayed home to help their mothers. But older boys followed the men, learning everything they would need to know to become adults in the village.

It was hot during the daytime, when the plateaus were lit by the sun, but nights were cold. The Pueblos ate warm cornbread, beans, and squash, and roasted meat over fires. Then they curled up in rabbit-skin robes and turkey-feather blankets and went to sleep because at sunrise they would start another long day.

But guess what these hardworking people did in their free time, Laurie? They played games! Running races, dart-throwing contests, and ball games were all popular. Of course the games were fun, but Pueblos also believed that these games were invented by the gods. So playing them pleased the gods and helped keep rivers flowing, rain falling, and the sun shining in the sky. When I get back, let's see if playing kickball every day will keep the gods happy and bring us lots of good sledding snow this winter!
Missing you,
Grandpa
P.S. I'll send you an email from the next site.
Laurie ran upstairs to the computer in the study. In her inbox was an e-card from Grandpa.

Laurie—I'm in Mesa Verde National Park in Colorado. Here Pueblos farmed, built houses, wove baskets, and performed rain dances. But in the 1200s, they moved down into the cliffs and built their homes into the steep walls of canyons, perhaps for protection. These peaceful people spent their time making pottery and offering respect to the gods. Then, about a hundred years later, they mysteriously left Mesa Verde forever.

Were they escaping something or had they simply outgrown their homes? No one knows. They continued to live nearby until the Spanish arrived in the 1500s and forced the Pueblos to leave their homes yet again. But Pueblo ancestors still live in the Southwest. In fact, I'll meet some modern Pueblos tomorrow at a ceremony! See you soon! –Grandpa
Laurie looked at the photograph on the e-card. She couldn't imagine climbing in and out of that big canyon every day just to get home. The Pueblos must have been so strong!
Laurie heard the front door open. "Laurie! Are you home? Sorry I'm late!" Mom called.
"I'm up here, Mom! I got mail from Grandpa in New Mexico!"

"Look what I made at school today!" Laurie said, coming into the study. "Since we're celebrating the explorer Christopher Columbus on Monday, we made astrolabes." She proudly presented the paper astrolabe to Grandpa.
"You did a great job!" Grandpa admired her work. "You know what these were used for, right?"
"To measure a ship's distance from the equator," Laurie stated.

"Correct. Sailors back in Columbus' time didn't have GPS or even a complete map of the earth! So they used interesting instruments to measure time and distance. In fact, I got something today that Columbus used on his voyage too." Grandpa picked up an hourglass on his desk. "This hourglass is similar to the ones fifteenth century Europeans used to keep time. Back then, one turn of the glass measured thirty minutes, but this one is a little smaller," he said. "A student in my Artifacts from the New World class made it."
"What's that class about?" Laurie wanted to know.
"Well, we examine artifacts that tell the story of Europeans landing in the New World. But I always begin with a quick history of the age of exploration."
"Quick? How quick?" Laurie flipped the hourglass over and grinned at Grandpa.

Grandpa grinned back, accepting the challenge. "In the 1400s trade was the fastest and easiest way to become rich. European explorers were discovering cities in Africa and Asia that produced spices, gold, silk, ivory, and precious gems. Spices like pepper and cinnamon were just being introduced to Europeans; if you could bring back a ship full of them, you could easily pay for the entire cost of your journey. The Portuguese were great shipbuilders and sailed often to Africa. So when Christopher Columbus thought he could sail west and find a shorter sea route to Asia, he asked the king of Portugal to sponsor him. But the king rejected Columbus' request. The explorer then traveled to Spain, where he asked Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand to support him. At first the rulers were hesitant, but the race for exploration had begun, and they didn't want to be left behind.

"So Isabella and Ferdinand gave Columbus three ships, ninety sailors, and lots of salted fish, biscuits, and water for the journey. The men set out on August 3, 1492. After two months, with still no sight of Asia, the crews nearly rebelled against Columbus and planned to kill him. Luckily for Columbus, on October 12, they landed on an island he believed was part of India. He named it San Salvador and called the people there Indians. But really, he was in the Caribbean, on an island called Guanahani. Its native people, the Tainos, were friendly, and the Spaniards were intrigued by their red face paint and gold earrings. The land was hot and humid, and the Tainos slept outside in hanging nets they called hammocks."
"I love hammocks!" Laurie blurted out.

"They're perfect on a summer day, aren't they?" Grandpa smiled. "The Europeans thought so too, and they brought hammocks, as well as canoes, tobacco, and other things they'd never seen, back to Spain. Columbus didn't find the gold he had hoped for. But he continued to claim nearby islands and govern them for Spain—even though people with their own societies and cultures already lived there. Hmph!" Grandpa shook his head before continuing. "His first journey was praised, but during his lifetime, Columbus never received the fame he gets today. Many Spanish rebelled against him, and Columbus treated the Tainos so poorly that there was no hope for peace between the natives and the Spanish. For example, Columbus turned the Tainos into slaves and forced them to find gold. If they didn't, he had them killed. Cruelty like that, along with diseases the Spanish brought from Europe, killed half the Taino population within two years. Disappointed in his abilities as a governor, Isabella and Ferdinand took away Columbus' privilege to govern the new lands.

"But Columbus Day is still a holiday in the U.S.—even though Columbus never reached North America. In fact, some think he wasn't even the first person to sail to the Caribbean. Oral histories tell of West Africans from the Mali kingdom setting out to explore the western seas, and of Chinese expeditions as well. But when Columbus reached land, he proved the existence of a land mass west of Europe, and that's why he's so famous."
"Grandpa, if Columbus gets credit for finding America, how come the Americas aren't called the Columbuses?" Laurie asked, puzzled.

"Well, a man named Amerigo Vespucci published a theory that the land wasn't Asia, but a new continent. So a mapmaker named the land 'America,' after Amerigo. Vespucci was a merchant and explorer who sailed to the South American coasts," Grandpa answered.
"So who discovered North America?" Laurie asked.

"It depends on what you mean by 'discovered,'" Grandpa said with a chuckle. "Native Americans were here for thousands of years before Europeans arrived. But Leif Eriksson, a Viking, is usually considered the first European to sail across the Atlantic to North America. His expedition arrived in what's now Canada in the year 1000. But since Leif didn't establish long-lasting colonies and governments, John Cabot, who sailed from England, is often considered the first European to claim North American land. He arrived in Canada in 1497."

"Time!" Laurie called. The hourglass was empty. "I hope you’re finished because I already have too much to think about. After hearing about the Tainos, I'm not sure if we should celebrate Columbus as a hero," Laurie admitted.
"Yes. Sometimes history teaches you unpleasant things," Grandpa answered. "But knowing both the good and the bad makes you smarter. Do you agree?"
"I agree," Laurie said. "I'm glad you're smart. I hope I will be too one day. See you at dinner?"
"See you at dinner." And Grandpa watched with a smile as his granddaughter walked away with a crinkled brow, no doubt still questioning who really discovered America.

17.title: The Samurai and Warlords Meet the Black Ships

paragraphs.text: Laurie had just gotten home from school when Grandpa appeared, holding a tray of tea and cookies.
"Welcome home, Laurie! You're just the girl I'm looking for. May I invite you to the study for a snack?"
"Okay . . ." Laurie answered with a suspicious smile. What was Grandpa up to now?
"How do Japanese cookies and tea sound?" Grandpa asked, grinning.
"Good."
"Please follow me." Grandpa led the way upstairs and into the study.
"Whoa! What's all this?" Laurie exclaimed. On the floor was a large, colorful map. Small buildings, ships, bridges, and figurines were scattered around it.
"I need to attach all these bits and pieces to this map . . . by tomorrow! Can you help me?"
"Sure!" Laurie replied. "What's it for?"

"I'm presenting a unit at the high school on the social order of Japan during the Tokugawa period—from 1600 to 1867—when Japan was ruled by the powerful Tokugawa family. I'm going to use this map of Japan to show where things took place." Grandpa picked up a small wooden bridge. "For example, we'll use this to mark the capital, Edo, which is now called Tokyo. Edo was a busy place; merchants, craftsmen, and lots of samurai crossed over this bridge. So we'll need to put those figures around here."
"Samurai were warriors," Laurie stated. "Why were there so many of them?"

"Because the shogun—the top leader in Japan at the time—lived in Edo. He was a warlord who held even more power than the emperor. This is his castle, actually," Grandpa said, picking up a castle replica. "The shogun required that samurai lords from all across Japan live in Edo for part of every year. That was his way of keeping an eye on them."
"This is a samurai, right?" Laurie asked. She held up a man carrying a sword.

"Yep. Samurai could easily be recognized by their armor, swords, and hairstyles. This one was probably a middle-ranking samurai. He would have been employed by one of the samurai lords, who were landowners. For centuries there was no central government to keep Japan stable. So there were constant civil wars between lords to expand their land and power. Samurai were not only highly respected, they were considered necessary! The warrior samurai and their lords made up the highest social class in Japan back then."
Laurie picked up a figure of a skinny man wearing a triangular straw hat. "Where does this one go?"

"He's a rice farmer. We'll put him in the farmlands surrounding Edo. Farmers were in the next highest class. They were important because they took care of the crops that fed the nation. Rice was, and still is, the main food eaten by the Japanese. During the Tokugawa period, rice was so valuable that it was used to pay rent!

"This is a craftsman. Since he's holding this small bowl, he probably makes lacquerware." Grandpa pointed to the tray he had brought up with the tea and cookies. "This is Japanese lacquerware. The Japanese carved items out of wood and then coated them with a shiny gloss. They perfected this art on their bowls and boxes and things. Anyway, this craftsman would be in the third social class, along with weavers, sword makers, and carpenters . . .
"That guy you're holding would probably fit into the last class."
"It looks like he's carrying lots of stuff," Laurie said.

"He's a merchant. In ancient and medieval Japan, merchants were at the bottom of the social hierarchy. In a culture that valued hard work, making money off someone else's labor wasn't as respectable as doing the labor yourself. But people began realizing that merchants were a key part of the economy, and merchants' value grew. Without them, cities might not have developed so quickly."
Laurie nodded as she added a cherry tree near the shogun's castle.

"This medieval Japanese society had a rigid class system, but it was also peaceful. The civil wars ended when the Tokugawa family claimed control over all the other warlords. Big cities developed and prospered; universities were built for high-ranking samurai; and arts like poetry, literature, painting, and lacquerware expressed Japanese culture.

"The Tokugawa shogun thought the best way to preserve this peace and stability was to close Japan off from other countries, particularly Western countries, which had a history of creating Christian empires and trading colonies. So foreigners weren't usually allowed in Japan."
"Then who's this guy? He doesn't look Japanese!" Laurie exclaimed, picking up a white man dressed in a military uniform.

"Ha! You found him! That's Commodore Perry," Grandpa said. "Despite Japan's wishes, the United States really wanted Japan to open its ports to their traders and sailors. In 1853 they sent Perry over with four armed, black naval ships. They warned the Japanese that if ports weren't opened, they would fire!"
"What did the Japanese do then?"

"Intimidated by the guns and steamships—which were new to the Japanese—they signed an agreement with the U.S. After that things changed rapidly. In 1867 the shogun resigned, and the emperor suddenly died. Then a young emperor called Meiji came to power. Emperor Meiji realized that if Japan wanted to keep itself safe in the modern world, it would need Western technology. So the Japanese imported ideas about education, politics, and science from the United States and Europe. But this map only covers the Tokugawa era. What do you say—are we finished?"

Laurie scanned the map, now speckled with people and buildings. "I think so," she replied. "Tokugawa Japan looks like it might have been an interesting place to visit . . . except I wouldn't have been allowed to enter the country!"

Grandpa chuckled. "You're absolutely right. Well, thank you, Laurie. I couldn't have done it without you. Now how about our snack?" he said. "In Japan, before you begin eating, you say itadakimasu! So on the count of three, ready? One, two, three—"
" Itadakimasu !" they both cried and reached for their cookies.

18.title: The American Revolution and a Brave Red Riding Hood

paragraphs.text: "Are you excited about your field trip?" Grandpa asked Laurie as they waited for the school bus.

Laurie shrugged. "I guess so. We're just visiting George Washington's headquarters in New Jersey during the American Revolution. Then we're riding horses through some woods where Washington's soldiers camped."

"That sounds great!" Grandpa said. "The American Revolution is my favorite part of American history. It was an exciting time when colonists were figuring out who they were and what they wanted from their government. When it was all over, they had founded a new country."
Laurie couldn't help smiling. As usual Grandpa was enthusiastic about something in history!
"I know the Revolution had something to do with tea and taxes," she said to him. "But what were the colonists really fighting about?"

"Independence and the right to decide how they were governed. Remember, what we know now as American states were British colonies back then. The founders and original colonists had come from England. So everyone, even people born in America, were British citizens governed by the British king—King George III.But he lived in England. Many colonists started grumbling that he couldn't possibly know what was best for the colonies when he was so far away.

"The really loud grumbling started when King George created the Stamp Act in 1765. This act said that any paper good sold in the colonies had to have a stamp on it, and the stamp had to be purchased from a British official. It was basically a tax paid to England. So the colonists protested this. 'No taxation without representation,' they said. That meant: you can't tax us unless we agree on the law together. Then England expanded the tax to include glass, tea, and other things. So the colonists decided to boycott British goods. England didn't like this, and sent soldiers to the colonies to keep things in order. The war for independence officially broke out in 1775. The next year the founding fathers of the United States wrote the Declaration of Independence. This document explained everything that the Americans were fighting for: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. They wanted to be completely free from British rule."
The school bus rumbled up the street.
"I'm sure you'll learn everything that happened after that on your field trip! Have fun!"
At four o'clock, Grandpa heard feet pounding on the steps. "How was it?" Grandpa asked as his granddaughter bounced into the room.
"So much fun!" Laurie answered. "I got you something." She held out a brown paper bag.
"Thanks!"

"It's a quill pen and some ink." Laurie showed him how to use it. "First, cut the tip of the quill with a knife to make a slanted edge. Then, dip that end in the ink bottle. That's how the colonists wrote. Cool, huh? The park ranger who gave us our tour taught me that."
"I bet you learned a lot today. Now you probably know more than I do about George Washington and the American Revolution," Grandpa said, grinning.

"No!" Laurie protested. "But I did learn that George Washington was a plantation owner from Virginia. When the colonists gathered to fight the British, they started an army called the Continental Army. George Washington became the commander. He led the soldiers through almost ten years of fighting, moving from colony to colony, until all the important areas were won. When the war ended, the colonists, who were now Americans, asked him to be their first president."
"I couldn't have said it better," Grandpa said proudly. "Now tell me something else you learned today," he said. "Something that really interested you."
Laurie thought a moment. "The story of Tempe Wick."
"Tempe Wick? That sounds like a story I don't know."

"Tempe Wick was a colonial girl who lived on her family's farm, called Wick Farm, in New Jersey. Tempe loved horses and wasn't afraid of anything. She was also a proud patriot who believed in the Revolution.

"During the war, Washington sent thirteen thousand soldiers to the woods around Wick Farm. They cleared the land and built log cabins to live in. But winter in New Jersey was cold and snowy. The soldiers were freezing, hungry, and tired.
The war seemed like it would never end. Sometimes the soldiers were bad. They stole food from nearby farms, and demanded that people give their best horses to them.

"One day Tempe was out riding her favorite horse, Colonel, when some Continental soldiers stopped her. They had just rebelled against their general and were abandoning their camp. They told her that Colonel was a beautiful horse. Then they grabbed his reins and said they wanted him! But Tempe didn't give in to their bullying. She didn't even get off her horse. As soon as they let go of the reins, she galloped away!

"Tempe knew the soldiers were following her. She was sure they'd come to the farm and take Colonel away. So she made a plan to fool the soldiers. Instead of putting Colonel in the stable, she led him into her bedroom! When the soldiers came to search the farm, they never thought to look in the house. The soldiers left empty-handed, and Tempe Wick got to keep her dear Colonel."
Laurie smiled. "And I got to see her beautiful red cape! The very same cape she wore that winter. I can just imagine her riding through the woods like Little Red Riding Hood."

Grandpa laughed loudly and clapped. "That's a great story!" he said. "I like it because it's about a young girl like you. She was proud to support the Continental soldiers, but she was also brave enough to stand up to them when they did something wrong."
"Kind of like how the colonists stood up to the British," Laurie said. "They were courageous, proud of their colonies, and fought to protect their rights."
"Exactly," Grandpa agreed. "You told that story very well, Laurie."
"Thanks, Grandpa."
"No, thank you —my little historian."

19.title: Tulips Take Over the Ottoman Empire

paragraphs.text: Laurie and Grandpa were reading quietly together on the couch, when Laurie suddenly jumped up. "I almost forgot! Our teacher gave us each a tulip bulb today. She said if we plant it now, it should bloom in the spring." Laurie reached into her backpack.
"Perfect. I was just reading some poetry by an eighteenth-century Turkish poet," Grandpa said, smiling dreamily.
Laurie stared at her grandpa. "I said I got a tulip bulb today."
Grandpa turned to her with the dreamy smile still on his face. "Do you know where tulips come from?" he asked.
"Holland?"
"Nope. Turkey. And the word 'tulip' comes from the Turkish word for turban because tulip bulbs and buds look like turbans, don't they?"
Laurie smiled as she examined the bulb in her hand. "You're right!"

"The period from 1718 to 1730 is known in Ottoman history as the Tulip Era. It was a time of peace for the Turkish Ottoman Empire, when the arts, culture, and architecture flourished. And—your bulb reminded me of this—tulip mania swept over the empire. Everyone, including the ruler, Sultan Ahmed III, was absolutely obsessed with tulips."
"How funny," Laurie said. "So is a sultan like a king?"

"Yes, a sultan is the ruler of a Muslim empire. The Ottoman Empire began in 1300 when a Muslim prince named Osman claimed a small area of land in western Turkey. Osman fought to expand his territory, and after he died, his son continued the expansion. Many years and many wars later, the Ottoman Empire had conquered neighboring Muslim dynasties in the Middle East, and most of the Eastern Roman Empire too. By the seventeenth century, the Ottomans controlled parts of Europe, Africa, and Asia. And the empire was always ruled by a sultan who was a male descendant of Osman.

"Sultans had luxurious lives. They lived in the best houses, wore the finest clothes, and ate the most delicious foods in the empire. They were also extremely sheltered from their people. In the 1400s Sultan Mehmed II conquered the city of Istanbul, made it the capital, and ordered a huge palace to be built there. The palace was called Topkapi. It was like a mini city, with multiple buildings, courtyards, mosques, and towers. This huge palace kept the sultan almost completely separated from his officials, soldiers, and subjects.

"But things change from generation to generation, and in the 1700s Sultan Ahmed III didn't like feeling locked up in stuffy, old Topkapi. He loved to celebrate and have parties. And he wanted to do this outside the palace. His grand vizier at the time—"
"What's a grand vizier?" Laurie interrupted.

"The grand vizier was the highest official in the Ottoman Empire after the sultan. He represented the sultan and was also the ruler's main adviser. The grand vizier was so important that only the sultan could hire or fire him.

"So the grand vizier suggested that the sultan build new royal palaces, along with mosques and public fountains that could be enjoyed by everyone. Not only would this make the sultan happy, but it would make him popular! You've heard of the French Palace of Versailles, haven't you?"
"Yep. Marie Antoinette lived there!" Laurie said, proud to know something important.

"Apparently Sultan Ahmed III was fascinated by the culture of Versailles. He had heard of the fancy parties and great banquets there. He wanted to bring a bit of that to the Ottoman Empire. So he built fountains and mosques that could be lit up at night. And he built a new palace with beautiful gardens.

The gardens were of course filled with tulips—tulips with round petals, tulips with pointed petals, tulips with brilliant yellow petals, and tulips streaked red and purple. Acrobats and entertainers performed in these gardens, while artists sketched, and poets wrote beneath the stars. And sometimes, on really special nights, the royal gardeners strapped candles onto the backs of turtles and released them in between the rows of tulips. The colorful flowers were illuminated all night."
"That sounds like fun," Laurie said. "Were kids allowed to go?"
"I'm sure the royal children were. At least until their bedtime. Sounds like a happy time to be living in the Ottoman Empire, doesn't it?" Grandpa asked.
"Only if you're invited to the parties!" Laurie said.

"Clever girl," Grandpa said, nodding. "Naturally the entire empire was not invited. And even though it was one of the wealthiest periods in Ottoman history, not everyone enjoyed such luxury. Peasants who were struggling to earn a living each day were unhappy. And so were the janissaries."
"Who were the janissaries?" Laurie asked.

"They were the Ottoman Empire's soldiers. During the empire's periods of conquest, they were quite respected. But in peace time, they didn't have anything to do! Some became gardeners or craftsmen, and others became restless. Eventually war broke out in the 1720s on the empire's borders with Iran. Ottoman troops went to Iran, but they failed to settle anything, and the Ottomans lost some territory. Unhappy with the sultan's weak military response, a group of janissaries revolted. The sultan was forced to resign and had the grand vizier executed. For a few weeks, there was chaos as the rebels burned palaces and destroyed signs of excess wealth. Finally the new sultan, Mahmud, put an end to the rebellion, but the happy times were over. Mahmud was occupied with wars against Iran and Russia for the rest of his reign, and didn't have much time for fancy garden parties."
"No more tulips for the Ottoman Empire?" Laurie asked, looking down at the bulb in her palm.
"Well, tulips are still a pride of Turkey and appear in lots of Turkish art. We could call them a legacy of Sultan Ahmed III's reign."
Laurie put the bulb on top of her head. "I'm going to go plant my turban now," she said, giggling. "See you later, Grandpa."

20.title: Early Days on the Wild Steppes of Russia

paragraphs.text: Grandpa heard Laurie in the hallway humming a tune from Tchaikovsky's Nutcracker Suite .
Laurie skipped into the study. "Oh, Grandpa, you should have come with Mom and Dad and me! The Nutcracker ballet was so good!"
"I wish I could have. But I had a lot of work to do, Laurie." Grandpa smiled warmly. "What's that you've got?" He pointed to the colorful book Laurie was holding.

"They were selling this at the theater. It retells the story of the Nutcracker and has photos from the ballet. Look!" She showed Grandpa a picture of a ballet dancer in a pink tutu. "I saw her dance today!" She pointed to a male dancer in a large, furry black hat. " He was my favorite!"
"Ha! The Cossack dancer!"
"I think they called him the Ukrainian dancer. He did amazing jumps!"

"Yes, the Cossacks, or the horsemen of the wild steppes, as they are sometimes called, are well-known for their energetic dancing! They were a rough group of nomadic fighters who lived in the unsettled land between the Volga, Don, and Dnieper Rivers of modern-day Russia and Ukraine."
"Fighters! Actually the dancer did have a sword." Laurie remembered. "It was fake though. What were they fighting for?"

"Well, many of them fought for Russia, who was trying to gain control over that area. Russia is huge now, isn't it? But like many other countries, it started out small and fought a lot to gain its territory. Way back in the 800s, royal Viking families began to form states and cities around those three rivers. One of the first states to be established was called Kievan Rus. From the ninth century to the twelfth century, Kievan Rus grew to become the largest, wealthiest state in the area."
"Does the name 'Russia' come from 'Kievan Rus'?" Laurie asked.

"It does! But it wasn't Russia yet. In the 1200s Genghis Khan and the Mongols invaded. Kievan Rus remained part of the Mongol Empire until the late 1400s. Then a prince from the rich trading city of Moscow organized the local people to resist Mongol rule. This prince was named Ivan III. Later, because he had freed his people from the Mongols, he became known as Ivan the Great."
"So now was it Russia?" Laurie wanted to know.
"Sure, now we can finally start calling it Russia. We could even call it the Russian Empire because Ivan IV—Ivan the Great's grandson—named himself Russia's first czar in 1547.

"Ivan the IV was a strong ruler who conquered lots of territory for Russia. But he is remembered as Ivan the Terrible because his rule was also one of the bloodiest in Russian history. You see, Ivan was incredibly worried about losing his authority. This made him wary of everyone, especially the rich Russian landowners, who held a lot of power. So he sent loyal servants to seize the noblemen's lands. And to guarantee that they would never fight him for it, he executed the landowners!

"Ivan the Terrible wanted to expand Russia's borders. He was particularly interested in defeating the Mongol hordes to the east and expanding Russia's territory all the way down the Volga River to the Caspian Sea. To do this he needed lots of men willing to fight for him."
"I know!" Laurie blurted out. "He used the Cossacks!" Laurie jumped up and pulled an imaginary sword from her hip.

"Right!" said Grandpa. "Luckily for Ivan, those wild horsemen lived right on the Russian borders. 'Cossack' comes from a word meaning free man. These men were considered free because they didn't belong to any of the states in the area. This meant they didn't follow any ruler's laws and didn't pay taxes to anyone. That probably doesn't sound like much to you, Laurie," Grandpa added, "but to adults that is a very big deal.

"Anyway, these Cossacks were usually peasant men who had left their original villages. They didn't like what life there had to offer them—most peasants in the Middle Ages lived practically as slaves. Out in the wild steppes, they became strong and excellent fighters—exactly what Ivan the Terrible needed. He hired these Cossacks to fight the Mongols. In exchange he promised to pay them and grant them continued independence. From then on the Cossacks became known as mercenaries. Do you know what a mercenary is?"
Laurie shook her head.

"A mercenary is someone who fights for pay. Besides the money they receive, they have no interest in the battles they fight," Grandpa explained. "Even after Ivan the Terrible, Russian rulers continued to employ the Cossacks, and they were responsible for helping Russia expand and protect its borders well into the eighteenth century."
"Well, they couldn't have been fighting all the time," Laurie remarked, glancing at her Nutcracker book. "When did they dance?"

"Good point. When they weren't fighting, the Cossacks liked to hunt, fish, drink, play music, and dance. Their dances became famous because of their incredible acrobatics. Cossack men were strong and fit, and they showed off their abilities by leaping into the air again and again."
"Like this?" Laurie squatted down and then jumped up, kicking one leg out.

"Yes! And like this!" Grandpa too jumped from his chair, crossed his arms in front of him, and kicked his feet out one at a time. Then the two linked arms, and began singing the theme from the Nutcracker Suite as they danced around the study. "One day we'll have to go to Ukraine and see a real performance by modern Cossacks!" Grandpa shouted joyfully.
"Yeah!" Laurie answered.
Suddenly there was a loud knock. "What on earth is all that racket?" Mom demanded from outside the door.
Grandpa and Laurie abruptly stopped dancing. Then they looked at each other and burst out laughing.
"For a 65-year-old archaeologist, Grandpa is pretty fun to hang out with," Laurie thought. And she was glad to be his granddaughter.
